---
title: Define a tool
description: A tool is the function that does the work, plus an optional hint about which control it belongs to. Nothing is added to your JSX.
sidebar:
  label: 1. Define a tool
---

A tool is something an agent can do on your page. You write one as **`execute`**, the function that does the work,
plus an optional **`target`** when the cursor needs to be told which control the tool belongs to. Nothing is added to
your JSX for the cursor: no attribute, no ref, no id.

:::note[shadcn/ui and React Hook Form are optional]
The Build examples use [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com) components and React Hook Form, because that is how most
React apps are built today. Each page says which components its examples use; this one uses only the button:

```package-install
npx shadcn@latest add button
```

Any component library, or plain elements, works the same: the cursor finds a control by its role and name.
:::

## A complete example

One function, two callers. Write the tool where its work lives, and pick the tab that fits:

- **`useWebTool`**, in a component: the tool is on while the component is on the page, and `execute` reads the
  component's own state.
- **`defineWebTool`**, in a module of its own: the tool belongs to the whole app, reads a store, and imports no
  React, so a server file can import it too. The provider registers it.

Both take the same options.

Either way, when an agent calls `clear_cart`, the cursor finds the button named "Clear cart", parks on it because of
`requireConfirmation`, and the work runs after the person's own click. What `execute` returns is the agent's answer.

A `defineWebTool` tool is registered by handing it to the provider (`tools={{ clearCart }}`), which is the subject of
[Tools across your app](/build/tools-across-your-app). A `useWebTool` tool registers itself.

## How the cursor finds the control

The cursor needs one thing from a tool: which control on the page it belongs to. It looks for it by role and name,
the way a screen reader names things.

- **The name it looks for is the tool's `title`**, or its `id` read as words (`clear_cart` is "clear cart"), among
  buttons, links, tabs, menu items and switches.
- **A control's name is its accessible name**: `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, its `<label>`, its `placeholder`,
  then its visible text, `alt` and `title`. Case and extra spaces do not matter, and an exact match beats one that
  only starts with the name ("Place order" finds "Place order · $46.00").
- **Icon-only buttons need an `aria-label`.** It is their name for the cursor, and for screen readers.
- **No control, no cursor.** A tool with nothing to point at runs at once, unseen, which is right for a read like
  `get_cart`. In development, the console says so once for any other tool.

## When the control depends on the call

Say which control with `target`: a locator, a CSS selector, or a function of the call's input that returns either.
Here each row has its own button, so the tool picks one per call.

| `target` | Example | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| A locator `{ role?, name?, within? }` | `{ role: "button", name: "Empty the cart" }` | The button's name differs from the tool's title. `name` takes a string or a RegExp; `within` narrows to a part of the page. |
| A CSS selector | `"#empty-cart"` | The control has an id and no good name. |
| A function of the input | `` ({ lineId }) => ({ role: "button", name: `Remove ${lines[lineId]}` }) `` | The control depends on the call, as above, or on the UI's language: `() => ({ role: "button", name: t("cart.clear") })`. |

## What the agent reads

Two things reach the agent: the `description`, before it calls, and what `execute` returns, after.

- **`description`** is how the agent decides. Say what the tool does, when to use it, what it needs first and what
  comes next. [Writing tool descriptions](/concepts/tool-descriptions) has the four things to say.
- **The return value is the answer.** A sentence ("The cart is empty."), or data. Throw when the tool cannot do its
  job: the agent reads the message as an error result with a [code](/concepts/errors), and the cursor never moves for
  input that fails the schema.

## Try it

Open the devtools panel (bottom right, or **Alt+Shift+A**), expand `clear_cart` and press **Run**. Or call the tool
from the browser console, the way an agent would. `agent` is there in development, put there by the devtools.

```js
await agent.invoke("clear_cart");
```

Either way the cursor parks on **Clear cart** until you click it. Scroll or click while it travels: it gets out of the
way, and the tool still finishes.

## Options you'll use most

| Option | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `id` | The tool's name, unique on the page. Snake case reads best to agents: `clear_cart`. |
| `title` | A human name, and the name the cursor looks for. |
| `description` | What the agent reads to decide when to call it. |
| `inputSchema` | The tool's parameters, as a zod (or any Standard Schema) object or JSON Schema. [Tools with input](/build/tools-with-input). |
| `execute` | The work. Its return value is the agent's answer. |
| `target` | Which control, when the name is not enough. |
| `requireConfirmation` | Wait for the person's own click. [Confirm before it runs](/build/confirm-before-it-runs). |
| `readOnly`, `destructive`, `repeatable`, `external` | Say what kind of tool it is, in plain words. Agents read them as WebMCP annotations. |

Every option, with its type and default: [`useWebTool`](/reference/react/use-web-tool) and
[`defineWebTool`](/reference/core/define-web-tool).
